summary: Describes three trust models and the threats relevant to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. It notes that IPsec AH was prescribed but limited to manual keying. The goal is to define requirements for securing Neighbor Discovery. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 devices use Neighbor Discovery messages to learn about nearby devices and routers. This memo describes three kinds of network trust and the attacks that a method for protecting those messages needs to handle.

subtitle: Three network trust settings and the attacks a secure IPv6 Neighbor Discovery design must address.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and address autoconfiguration let nodes learn local addresses and routers, but false messages can redirect traffic or deny service. The suggested IPsec Authentication Header protection lacked a workable automatic key-management method.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines three trust models and catalogs Neighbor Discovery and Router Discovery threats in each setting.
tldr.outcome: It provides threat and trust requirements for work on Secure Neighbor Discovery; it does not define a security protocol.

today: RFC 3756 is an Informational document published in May 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo itself describes a threat analysis intended to inform SEND work.

sections.title: Why Neighbor Discovery Needs Protection
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Address Autoconfiguration help nodes learn which link-layer address belongs to a local IP address, which routers are present, and which prefixes those routers serve. Existing specifications suggested IPsec Authentication Header (AH) protection but did not define how to manage the keys.

The memo explains that manual key setup is impractical for devices joining networks, especially public networks where a visiting host may have no prior trust relationship. It also notes that Neighbor Discovery uses a large range of solicited-node multicast addresses, making preconfiguring security associations for every possible address unmanageable.

The document's purpose is to describe network trust settings and threats that a Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) design should address. Its examples of possible mechanisms are illustrative and do not express a preference.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbor Discovery helps an IPv6 device learn who and what is on its local network. Protecting those messages requires a way to establish trust and keys even when a device is new to the network.

sections.title: Why Manual Keying Falls Short
sections.content:
A host may need Neighbor Discovery to get initial access to a link, yet IPsec AH protection requires security associations and keys. A host joining a public or roaming network may not have them configured in advance. The memo describes a key-management loop: IKE needs an IP address, IKE establishes IPsec security associations, and those associations are needed to configure an address.

Preconfiguring associations also scales poorly because Neighbor Discovery uses fixed multicast addresses and a range of 16 million solicited-node multicast addresses. The memo presents this as a practical obstacle to using manual security associations for every possible address.
sections.plainLanguage: A device may need network access before it can set up the keys that protect network discovery. Setting up keys for every possible discovery address in advance would also be impractical.

sections.title: Three Trust Models
sections.content:
The memo uses “trust” to mean a shared belief that other parties will behave correctly. It separates Neighbor Discovery operations that do not primarily involve routers from Router Discovery operations that do. It then describes three settings:

  1. Corporate intranet: authenticated nodes under one administration are assumed to behave correctly. Physical or link-layer protection may be enough if nodes are not compromised, though further protection can limit damage from a compromised node.
  2. Operator-run public network: clients trust the operator's router to forward traffic correctly, but do not trust other clients. Link-layer security alone may not prevent every threat.
  3. Ad hoc network: nodes have no prior trust in one another or a trusted third party, so traditional authentication based on an existing relationship does not apply. Self-identifying techniques may help verify that a node uses an address it generated itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo distinguishes a managed office network, a public network where users trust the operator but not one another, and a network of strangers. Each setting needs to handle a different level of trust.

sections.title: Threats to Neighbors and Addresses
sections.content:
The memo groups threats as traffic redirection, denial of service (DoS), or flooding DoS. Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement spoofing can replace an address-to-link-layer mapping and send packets elsewhere. Neighbor Unreachability Detection can be disrupted by forged replies, and false responses to Duplicate Address Detection can prevent a joining node from using an address.

Some attacks can exploit Router Advertisements to pose as a default router, remove a real router, install false on-link or address-configuration prefixes, or change parameters such as the hop limit. A spoofed Redirect can send a host's packets to an attacker. False address configuration can also affect DNS if a host registers the resulting address.

Neighbor and Router Discovery messages can be replayed. The memo describes nonces for request-reply exchanges and timestamps or counters for standalone messages as ways to resist replay. It also describes a resource-exhaustion attack in which an attacker makes a last-hop router send many Neighbor Solicitations for fabricated addresses, filling its unresolved-neighbor state.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can send false messages that change where traffic goes, stop a device from obtaining an address, or overload a router. Captured messages can also be replayed, so protection must check that messages are fresh.

sections.title: How the Threat Summary Is Read
sections.content:
The attack summary table compares threats across the three trust models. A dash means the threat is absent or not a concern in that model. A plus sign means the threat is present and the authors believe a solution is known in principle; it does not mean a standardized solution is ready to use. “R” means the authors consider solving the threat a research problem.

The table and threat descriptions are intended to establish requirements for securing IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. The RFC is an Informational analysis, not the protection protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The summary marks whether each attack applies in each trust setting and whether a solution is known in principle. A plus sign does not mean that a finished standard already solves the problem.
